.ENV.EXAMPLE DRIFT CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Does your .env.example still match what the code actually reads?

Paste your .env.example and your source code and see every environment variable the code reads (process.env, os.getenv/os.environ, ENV[], System.getenv) that the example file never mentions — the failure a new contributor hits the moment they run cp .env.example .env and start the app — plus every variable the example file declares that nothing reads anymore.

Nothing is uploaded. Both text boxes are parsed in this browser and never leave your device. This is a name diff, not a secrets scanner: it never reads or shows a value, only variable names.

1. Paste your files

2. What drifted

VariableStatusDetail

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file — and it can walk a whole source tree in one pass, skipping node_modules, .git, and similar:

node cli.mjs check --example .env.example src               # one directory, human-readable
node cli.mjs check --example .env.example . --json             # whole tree, machine-readable
node cli.mjs check --example .env.example src app.py           # a mix of directories and files
node cli.mjs check --example .env.example src --strict          # also fail on unused declared vars

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install. It reads only the local files/directories you name: no network call, ever. Exits 1 if any variable is read in code but missing from the example file, so it works as a PR gate on the same review that adds the read.

What's scanned, per language

LanguagePatterns matched

Matched line by line, name only — the tool never reads or reports a value on either side. Shell scripts, YAML, and Docker Compose files are not scanned in v0; paste the application source that actually reads the variable instead.

More: why example files drift from the code that reads them, and where to wire this into CI. Already running dotenv-linter on your .env files? See how the two compare -- they check different things and compose. Already grep for process.env by hand? See what a quick grep misses.

Common questions

Why does a missing .env.example variable matter so much?

It is usually the very first command a new contributor or a CI runner executes after cloning: copy the example file to .env, then start the app. A variable the code reads but the example file never mentions means that first run crashes immediately, and it reads as "this project is broken" rather than as what it actually is, a doc that fell one pull request behind.

Why would the example file and the code ever disagree?

A pull request adds a new process.env.FOO read (a new API key, a new feature flag) and nobody remembers to add FOO to .env.example in the same review. Nothing mechanical keeps the two in sync unless something checks -- the same reason lockfiles and changelogs drift, just with a sharper, more immediate failure the moment someone new clones the repo.

Is this a secrets scanner?

No. It never reads or reports a value on either side, only variable names -- whether a name is declared in the example file and whether that same name is read anywhere in the scanned code. It cannot see, and does not want to see, what a real .env file (which this tool never asks for) actually contains.

Is my code uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses the text you paste entirely in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads only local files -- no network call, ever.

It reports whether a variable name appears on both sides of a text diff — nothing more, and it is not a guarantee that your configuration is complete or safe. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The text you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a pass on the same repo: Structured Data Drift Check asks the same "does the doc still match the code" question about a page's JSON-LD instead of an env file, and package.json Exports Drift Check asks it about a package's exports map instead — both with the same deterministic, no-upload shape. Checking Terraform instead of application config? Terraform Plan Secret Exposure Check is a related but explicitly different job — not a `.env` reader, a check for secret-shaped values your provider schema forgot to mark sensitive. Checking your AI coding agent's own instructions instead of your app's config? Agent Instructions Drift Check asks the same drift question about AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md — broken file references, undefined npm scripts, and known interpreter-mismatch shell footguns.

Wondering which folders of that repo only one person ever touched? Git Bus Factor Check reads your git log and flags folders whose main contributor has gone quiet, with the same no-upload shape.

Calling an LLM API from that code? LLM Call Cost Scan is the same zero-upload shape for a different bug: it reads the source for OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini calls with no output cap, calls inside loops, premium models and retired model names.

vs-dotenv-linter.html.text:
← .env.example Drift Check

This tool vs. dotenv-linter

dotenv-linter is a free, open-source command-line tool, written in Rust, that checks a single .env file against its own formatting rules. Its documentation lists 14 checks -- duplicated key, ending blank line, extra blank line, incorrect delimiter, key without value, leading character, lowercase key, quote character, schema violation, space character, substitution key, trailing whitespace, unordered key, and value without quotes -- and it can automatically fix many of them. Every one of those checks looks inward, at the file's own internal consistency. None of them open a source file, and none of them know whether a declared variable is read by any code anywhere.

This tool checks a different pair of things entirely, and never looks at a file's own formatting. It parses an .env.example file's declared variable names, scans source code for process.env.FOO (JavaScript/TypeScript), os.getenv / os.environ (Python), ENV[] (Ruby), and System.getenv (Java) reads, and diffs the two lists -- naming every variable the code reads that the example file never mentions, and, in --strict mode, every variable the example file declares that nothing reads anymore. A perfectly tidy, alphabetised, consistently-quoted .env.example that dotenv-linter would pass cleanly can still be missing three variables the code reads; that gap is exactly what this tool is built to catch.

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Catch duplicate keys, inconsistent quoting, unordered keys, or a key with no value in one .env file. dotenv-linter -- that is exactly its 14-check list, and it can auto-fix most of them.
Find out whether .env.example's declared names actually match what the code reads. This tool -- dotenv-linter's checks never open a source file, so it cannot see this at all.
Stop a new contributor's cp .env.example .env && npm start from crashing on a variable the example file forgot. This tool, wired into CI as a gate on the same PR that adds the read.
Work across JavaScript, Python, Ruby, and Java in one repo. This tool's source scan covers all four; dotenv-linter's checks are language-agnostic because they never read source code in the first place.
Keep an .env or .env.example file's own syntax clean before committing it. dotenv-linter -- this tool never checks formatting and would not notice a duplicate key.

These compose rather than compete, and cost nothing to run together: dotenv-linter as a fast pre-commit or CI step for the example file's own hygiene, and this tool's cli.mjs in the same CI job checking that the file's contents still match the code. Neither one makes the other redundant, and a repo that only runs one is only checking half the problem.

Common questions

Should I use this tool or dotenv-linter?

Most repos that care about this will want both, because they check different things. dotenv-linter is a fast, dependency-free command-line tool, written in Rust, that lints one .env file against 14 formatting rules -- duplicate keys, unordered keys, inconsistent quoting, trailing whitespace, a key without a value, and similar -- and can auto-fix many of them. It never looks at your application code. This tool does the opposite: it never checks an .env file's formatting at all, and instead diffs the variable names declared in .env.example against the process.env.FOO / os.getenv / ENV[] / System.getenv reads actually found in your source code across JavaScript, Python, Ruby, and Java, naming every variable the code reads that the example file never mentions. Run dotenv-linter to keep one file's syntax clean. Run this tool to catch the example file quietly falling behind the code that reads it -- the bug that crashes a new contributor's first cp .env.example .env.

Does this replace dotenv-linter?

No, and it is not trying to. dotenv-linter's 14 checks (duplicated key, unordered key, quote character, trailing whitespace, key without value, and so on) all look inward at one file's own formatting; none of them read your application source code or know whether a declared variable is used anywhere. This tool never checks formatting at all -- a perfectly tidy .env.example, sorted and quoted exactly right, can still be missing three variables the code reads, and this tool is the one that would catch that. They compose: a repo can run both in the same CI job and get two independent, non-overlapping checks for the price of two free tools.

Is this page affiliated with dotenv-linter?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by the dotenv-linter project or its maintainers. dotenv-linter is named here only to describe what this tool is and is not, based on dotenv-linter's own public documentation; check its repository for what it currently supports.

vs-grepping-the-codebase-by-hand.html.text:
← Back to .env.example Drift Check

.env.example Drift Check vs. grepping the codebase by hand

grep -rn "process\.env\." src/ genuinely works for the case it is written for, and it is the method most people already reach for. This page names no product or company being compared against: grepping is a generic manual habit, not a competing tool.

CaseGrepping by handThis tool
A dot-notation read, process.env.API_KEYCorrectly caught by a grep written for the dot patternCorrectly caught the same way, as one of the JavaScript/TypeScript patterns
A bracket-notation read, process.env["AWS_REGION"]Invisible to a grep tuned for process\.env\. -- no match, no warning that anything was skippedMatched by a separate bracket-notation pattern, checked every time regardless of which notation a file uses
A polyglot repo with a JavaScript frontend and a Python or Ruby serviceNeeds a second, correctly-written grep per language, run every time -- easy to run only the one for the file you are already looking atScans for all four languages' read patterns in the same pass, whether or not the repo mixes them
Cross-referencing 40 grep hits against 15 names in .env.exampleA manual set-difference held in your head -- the kind of exhaustive comparison people get wrong under time pressure, with no signal when they doA deterministic Map diff: exactly the names read in code but absent from the example file, every time
A variable declared in .env.example that nothing reads anymoreNobody checks this direction unless someone thinks to -- it produces no crash, just silently stale docs--strict flags every declared-but-unread name the same way, every run
Catching drift a PR introduces next monthA one-time audit answers for today; nothing re-runs it on the next commitcli.mjs wired into CI re-checks every PR that touches source or the example file

The gap that matters most: bracket notation has no shared substring with the dot pattern

process.env["AWS_REGION"] and process.env.AWS_REGION read the identical variable, but a grep pattern written to catch the second -- typically process\.env\.[A-Z_]+ or similar -- does not match the first at all. There is no partial hit, no warning line, nothing to notice: the bracket-notation read simply does not appear in the grep's output, and a review that trusts a clean grep pass has no way to tell the difference between "no missing variables" and "a whole notation this grep can't see." This tool's scanSource matches both notations as separate, always-checked patterns, so which style a given file happens to use does not change the result.

The gap that matters second: one grep per language, applied inconsistently

os.getenv("FOO"), os.environ["FOO"], ENV["FOO"], and System.getenv("FOO") are four more call shapes across three more languages, each needing its own grep pattern to catch. A repo that mixes a JavaScript frontend with a Python worker or a Ruby background service needs someone to remember, and correctly write, a separate grep for each one -- and it is the service nobody is currently staring at that a quick audit skips. This tool checks all of them in the same pass over whatever text it is handed, so the check does not depend on which language the person running it happens to be thinking about.

When to still check the codebase yourself

This is a fixed set of text patterns, not code evaluation -- it cannot see a variable name assembled at runtime (process.env[someVariable]), and it does not read shell scripts, YAML, or Docker Compose files at all, so a variable read only through one of those is invisible to it the same as it would be to a grep. Confirming a name outside its pattern list, and understanding a dynamically-built variable name, is still a job for reading the code yourself.

Common questions

What does grepping for process.env actually catch?

grep -rn "process\.env\." src/ finds every dot-notation read in one pass and is genuinely fast for a single-language JavaScript codebase. That case is real and this tool's engine.mjs matches it the same way, as one of its LANGUAGE_PATTERNS entries.

Why does a grep for process.env miss bracket-notation reads?

process.env["AWS_REGION"] and process.env['AWS_REGION'] both read the variable, but neither contains the literal substring process.env. followed directly by a bare name -- the dot-then-identifier pattern most people type into grep. A grep tuned for the dot-notation case does not match the bracket case at all, and it never announces the miss; the line simply never appears in the results.

Why does a grep audit not scale past one language?

process.env, os.getenv, os.environ[], ENV[], and System.getenv are five different call shapes across four languages. A repo with a JavaScript frontend and a Python worker needs two separate, correctly-written greps run every time, and it is easy to run the one for the language you are staring at and skip the other -- especially in a service you did not personally write.

Why is eyeballing grep hits against .env.example error-prone?

A real codebase's process.env reads run into the dozens once every file that touches configuration is counted, most of them already declared. The task is a manual set-difference: read down a list of hits, hold the .env.example file's declared names in your head, and notice the one name that is not on both sides. That kind of exhaustive comparison against a mental list is exactly the class of check people get wrong under time pressure, and a clean-looking grep pass gives no signal about whether it was done right.

Does this tool replace checking the codebase by hand entirely?

No. It scans for a fixed list of call-shape patterns in text and knows nothing about shell scripts, YAML, or Docker Compose files reading a variable through some other mechanism, and it never evaluates code -- a name built dynamically at runtime (process.env[someVariable]) is invisible to it the same as it would be to a grep. Confirming a variable name it did not catch, or one read through a mechanism outside its pattern list, is still a job for reading the code yourself.

why-env-example-files-drift-from-the-cod.text:
← Back to .env.example Drift Check

Why .env.example files drift from the code that reads them

.env.example (or .env.sample) exists to be a contract: clone the repo, copy it to .env, fill in real values, and the app has everything it needs. That contract only holds while the file's declared names exactly match the environment variables the code actually reads — and nothing about how most repos are built keeps that true on its own.

Why it happens: one file, edited on a different schedule than the code

A pull request adds a new integration and a new process.env.STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET read somewhere deep in a route handler. The change works, the tests pass (test environments often stub the value directly), and the PR merges. Updating .env.example in the same diff is a manual, easy-to-forget step that no build or type check enforces — a variable read and a variable declared are two separate authored artifacts with no mechanical link between them, the same shape as a changelog that quietly stops matching the commits it describes.

Why this bug is unusually visible, and unusually annoying

Most documentation drift is invisible until someone happens to read the stale section. This one is different: it fails the very first command a new contributor, a new environment, or a CI runner executes after cloning — cp .env.example .env followed by starting the app — with a crash or a confusing default that has nothing to do with what the person actually did wrong. It reads as "this project is broken" rather than as what it is, a doc that fell one pull request behind, and it costs exactly the person least equipped to debug it (someone new to the codebase) the most time figuring out.

What this tool checks, and what it deliberately doesn't

LanguagePatterns matched
JavaScript / TypeScriptprocess.env.FOO, process.env["FOO"]
Pythonos.getenv("FOO"), os.environ["FOO"], os.environ.get("FOO")
RubyENV["FOO"], ENV.fetch("FOO")
JavaSystem.getenv("FOO")

Deliberately excluded from v0: shell scripts, YAML/Compose files, and any environment read built dynamically rather than as a literal name in one of the patterns above. Matched one line at a time by design, so it is trivially explainable and does not need a language parser — the tradeoff is that a read split unusually across multiple lines will not be seen, which in practice is rare for this specific call shape.

Wiring it into CI as a gate

Run it on every pull request, pointed at the directory (or directories) that actually read environment variables:

- name: Check .env.example against actual env reads
  run: node ventures/env-example-drift-check/cli.mjs check --example .env.example src

The command exits non-zero if any variable is read in code but missing from the example file. Add --strict to also fail when the example file declares a variable nothing reads anymore — a softer signal (stale documentation, not a crash) worth a separate, less urgent gate.

Common questions

Isn't this just a linter rule?

ESLint and similar tools can flag process.env usage inside one language's own files, but none of the common ones diff those reads against a separate .env.example file's declared names, and none work across JavaScript, Python, Ruby, and Java in one pass. This tool is narrower and more specific than a general linter rule: it answers exactly one question, does the example file's variable list match what the code actually reads, for a repo that may mix languages.

Does this replace dotenv-linter or similar tools?

No, and it is not trying to. Tools like dotenv-linter check an .env file's own internal formatting (duplicate keys, inconsistent quoting, unordered keys). This tool checks a different pair entirely: the example file's declared names against the source code's actual reads. They compose -- run both.

What about variables read from a config object instead of process.env directly?

Not scanned in v0. A codebase that centralizes all environment reads into one config module (a common and good pattern) means most of the actual process.env.FOO calls live in one or two files, which is exactly where pointing the CLI at that module still works well; a config object built dynamically from a list of names, rather than named process.env.FOO calls, is outside what a deterministic text scan can see.

No warranty. This page and the tool it documents report whether a variable name appears on both sides of a text diff between an example file and scanned source code — nothing more. It is not security, legal, or engineering advice, and it is not a secrets scanner or a guarantee that your configuration is complete or safe. Verify by reading the actual files before relying on it. Back to the tool.
